title: Protecting plant health
summary: Identify diseases, pests, nutrient deficiencies and water stress. Natural recipes for biopesticides and biofertilizers (garlic, neem, fermented extracts).

pages.title: Healthy plants for abundant harvests
pages.text:
Abundant harvests start with **healthy plants**.

This module shows you how to recognize warning signs, use natural solutions and prevent problems on your growing beds.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Des plantes en bonne santé pour des récoltes abondantes

pages.title: Protecting plant health
pages.text: In this module, you will discover a simple method to diagnose the condition of your crops, respond effectively with **natural solutions** and durably prevent imbalances thanks to living soil.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Protéger la santé des plantes

pages.title: Understanding the different types of problems
pages.text: Before taking action or treating a crop, it is essential to correctly identify the origin of the problem so that you can give the most appropriate response.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Comprendre les différents types de problèmes

pages.title: The 4 main types of plant health problems
pages.text:
There are **4 main types** of problems that can affect the health of a plant:

1. **Diseases** (fungi, bacteria, viruses).
2. **Nutrient deficiencies** (lack or lock-up of nutrients).
3. **Insect pests** (pests that attack leaves, stems or fruits).
4. **Stress** (unsuitable climatic, water or planting conditions).
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les 4 grands types de problèmes de santé

pages.title: Recognizing a disease problem
pages.text: The first step of the diagnosis: learn to spot the signs of a disease, understand what favors it and adopt the right practices to protect your crops.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Reconnaître un problème lié à une maladie

pages.title: The origins of a disease
pages.text:
A **disease** is caused by a pathogenic microorganism that attacks the plant:

- a **fungus**,
- a **bacterium**,
- or a **virus**.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les origines d’une maladie

pages.title: Signs of disease to look for
pages.text:
A plant may be diseased if you observe one or more of the following symptoms:

- **Spots on the leaves**: black, white or brown.
- **Rot**: visible on fruits or roots.
- **Deformation**: distorted or curled leaves.
- **Permanent wilting**: even if the plant has received enough water.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Signes d’une maladie à observer

pages.title: Factors that favor diseases
pages.text:
Diseases are favored by:

- **Too much water**: overly frequent watering, constantly wet soil, long rainy spells.
- **Too little water**: a thirsty plant is less resistant to diseases.
- **Extreme heat or cold snaps**: sudden variations can weaken the plant and trigger diseases.
- **Lack of air between plants**: overly tight spacing encourages stagnant humidity and therefore diseases.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les facteurs qui favorisent les maladies

pages.title: What to do when a plant is diseased?
pages.text:
As soon as the first signs of disease appear, act quickly:

- **Cut**: remove the affected parts (diseased leaves, stems or fruits) to prevent spread.
- **Remove**: pull out the whole plant if it is too diseased and can no longer be saved.
- **Strengthen**: strengthen the plant and the soil with a light application of compost or compost tea.
- **Treat**: apply a natural treatment (garlic infusion, neem purin, baking soda…).

⚠️ **Warning**: do not leave diseased parts at the foot of the crops, so as not to contaminate neighboring plants.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Que faire quand une plante est malade ?

pages.title: Preventing the disease from coming back
pages.text:
To prevent the disease from returning to your growing beds, you can:

- **Thin out the foliage**: let air and light through to limit stagnant humidity.
- **Adjust watering**: water regularly without excess, preferably at the base of the plants.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Éviter le retour de la maladie

pages.title: Recognizing a nutrient deficiency problem
pages.text: The second type of problem: nutrient deficiencies. Learn to read the visual signs on the foliage and growth so you can feed your soil effectively.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Reconnaître un problème lié à une carence

pages.title: Signs of deficiency to look for
pages.text:
When a plant does not receive all the nutrients it needs, it quickly shows. A plant may be deficient if you observe:

- **Yellow leaves** (often at the bottom of the plant).
- **Small or deformed fruits**.
- **Red or purple stems**.
- **Leaves with dry, red or purple edges**.
- **Slow growth** and stunted plants.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Signes d’une carence à observer

pages.title: The causes of deficiencies
pages.text:
Deficiencies mainly appear in three situations:

- **Poor soil**: compost is absent or of poor quality.
- **Soil that is too compacted or poorly aerated**: water and nutrients cannot properly reach the roots.
- **Unbalanced pH** (acidity or alkalinity): when the soil is too acidic or too alkaline, it can lock up certain nutrients, even if they are present in the soil.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les causes des carences

pages.title: How to correct a deficiency?
pages.text:
To correct a deficiency and restart crop growth:

- **Strengthen**: add mature compost regularly (1 to 2 wheelbarrows per bed depending on the crop).
- **Treat**: use leaf purin (**neem**, **moringa**, nettle, comfrey…) to stimulate growth.
- **Test**: test the soil pH if the problem persists (pH paper or simple kit). If it is too acidic, you can correct it with a small amount of agricultural lime.
- **Analyze**: have a soil analysis done to supply the missing elements.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Comment corriger une carence ?

pages.title: Recognizing a problem caused by insect pests
pages.text: The third type of problem: insect pests. Detecting them early lets you intervene before the infestation jeopardizes the harvest.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Reconnaître un problème causé par des insectes nuisibles

pages.title: Signs of insect pest presence
pages.text:
Insect pests weaken plants, reduce harvests and transmit diseases. It is better to spot them early to limit damage:

- **Visible insects**: caterpillars, whiteflies, aphids, locusts, maggots…
- **Holes in the leaves**: eaten edges or round holes in the middle.
- **Damaged fruits**: pierced, rotten or gnawed before maturity.
- **Deformed or sticky leaves**: a sign of aphids.
- **Small tunnels** in the leaves or roots: worms, nematodes.
- **Presence of eggs** on stems or under leaves.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Signes de présence d’insectes nuisibles

pages.title: Plants to watch closely
pages.text:
Some plants are more vulnerable to pests and call for particular vigilance:

- **Young seedlings and young plants**, whose tender leaves are very attractive to insects.
- **Stressed or weakened plants**, which defend themselves less well.
- **Sensitive crops** such as cabbages, tomatoes, beans or okra, which are attacked more often.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les plantes à surveiller de près

pages.title: What to do in case of pests?
pages.text:
If you have spotted signs of pests on your growing beds:

- **Cut**: remove heavily attacked leaves to slow down the infestation.
- **Spray**: spray the plants with water to knock off the insect pests.
- **Protect**: install nets or fine mesh against flying insects.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Que faire en cas de ravageurs ?

pages.title: Preventing pests from coming back
pages.text:
To durably limit the return of pests:

- **Monitor**: regularly inspect under the leaves and around young shoots to spot problems from the start.
- **Plant repellents**: install basil, mint, lemongrass or marigolds next to the crops.
- **Attract beneficial insects**: encourage ladybugs or certain wasps, which eat pests. Place the insect pests on a plate near the crops along with seeds to attract birds: they will then come and pick the insect pests directly off the plants.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Éviter le retour des ravageurs

pages.title: Recognizing a stress-related problem
pages.text: The fourth type of problem: physiological stress. A plant that looks unwell is not always diseased or attacked by insects.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Reconnaître un problème lié à un stress

pages.title: Signs of stress in the plant
pages.text:
The plant seems unwell, but no pest or disease is visible. What if it is **stress**?

The main signs to look for are:

- It is **wilted in the middle of the day**, especially in hot weather.
- It has **stopped growing**.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Signes d’un stress chez la plante

pages.title: The causes of stress
pages.text:
Several environmental or cultural factors can cause stress in the plant:

- **Soil that is too hot or too cold**.
- **Extreme variations**: soil too dry or too wet.
- **Poorly done transplanting** or transplanting in full sun.
- **Transplanting too early or too late**.
- **Soil that is too compacted**: roots struggle to establish.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les causes du stress

pages.title: What to do in case of stress?
pages.text:
⚠️ **Warning**: wait before treating! Stress often disappears within **1 to 2 days** if the plant returns to good conditions.

If the stress persists, apply these simple practices:

- **Mulch**: apply mulch to retain moisture in the soil.
- **Water**: water regularly without excess.
- **Protect**: protect the plants with shade cloth (shade netting).
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Que faire en cas de stress ?

pages.title: Limiting problems through bio-intensive market gardening on living soil
pages.text: The best protection is still prevention. Discover how the practices of bio-intensive market gardening on living soil naturally strengthen the resistance of your crops.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Limiter les problèmes grâce au maraîchage bio-intensif en sol vivant

pages.title: A living soil for more resistant plants
pages.text:
**Bio-intensive market gardening on living soil** naturally strengthens plants and soil.

Result: plants are healthy and there are **fewer problems**.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Un sol vivant pour des plantes plus résistantes

pages.title: Planting well in bio-intensive market gardening
pages.text:
From planting onward, four simple rules help prevent many problems:

- **Choose varieties well** according to the season.
- **Respect planting distances** to let air and light circulate.
- **Combine complementary crops** through companion planting.
- **Practice crop rotation** to break disease and pest cycles.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Bien planter en maraîchage bio-intensif

pages.title: Maintaining your crops on living soil
pages.text:
Throughout the crop cycle, maintain the vitality of your plants and soil:

- **Apply compost regularly** or compost tea.
- **Mulch generously** to protect the soil and retain moisture.
- **Water gently with soft irrigation** on the growing beds and the paths.
- **Use insect nets** to protect sensitive crops.
- **Adjust the water supply** according to the plant's growth stage.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Entretenir ses cultures en sol vivant

pages.title: Making a natural treatment
pages.text: When prevention is not enough, simple natural preparations allow you to intervene without harming the living soil.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Fabriquer un traitement naturel

pages.title: Using plants to protect crops
pages.text:
If the problem persists despite preventive measures, a **natural treatment** is needed.

Certain local plants (neem, garlic, chili pepper, ginger…) can be turned into **purins** (fermented extracts), **infusions** or **decoctions** to effectively protect crops.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Utiliser les plantes pour protéger les cultures

pages.title: Key takeaways: preventing and protecting naturally
pages.text:
With a **living, well-fed soil**, **nets** to protect crops and **suitable natural treatments**, most problems can be prevented and managed without using chemical products.

By practicing good crop rotation and choosing varieties wisely, you also encourage more resistant plants and better harvests.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour À retenir : prévenir et protéger naturellement
